claim: KIF2C is expressed in multiple regions of the mouse brain.
source: Western blot analyses showed that KIF2C was expressed in multiple regions of the brain (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating KIF2C protein expression across different brain regions.

claim: KIF2C shows sustained high expression in the hippocampus throughout postnatal stages.
source: Western blot analyses showed that KIF2C was expressed in multiple regions of the brain (Figure 1A), and shows sustained high expression in the hippocampus throughout the postnatal stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing KIF2C expression levels across different postnatal developmental stages.

claim: KIF2C is detectable at DIV 3 in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: The results showed that KIF2C was expressed in a development-related pattern in cultured neurons: detectable at day in vitro 3 (DIV 3) and significantly increased at DIV 10.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis on cultured hippocampal neurons at different developmental stages (Figure 1C).

claim: KIF2C expression significantly increases at DIV 10 in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: The results showed that KIF2C was expressed in a development-related pattern in cultured neurons: detectable at day in vitro 3 (DIV 3) and significantly increased at DIV 10.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing increased KIF2C protein levels at DIV 10 (Figure 1C).

claim: KIF2C is enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD) fraction.
source: Moreover, the subcellular fractionation analysis showed an enrichment of KIF2C in the postsynaptic density (PSD) fraction (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data showing higher KIF2C levels in PSD fraction compared to other fractions.

claim: KIF2C colocalizes with the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 in cultured neurons.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of cultured neurons revealed KIF2C expression as granular puncta of different sizes along dendrites overlapping with the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 and presynaptic protein Bassoon (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing colocalization of KIF2C with PSD-95.

claim: KIF2C colocalizes with the presynaptic protein Bassoon in cultured neurons.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of cultured neurons revealed KIF2C expression as granular puncta of different sizes along dendrites overlapping with the postsynaptic marker PSD-95 and presynaptic protein Bassoon (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing colocalization of KIF2C with Bassoon.

claim: KIF2C knockdown does not affect spine density in cultured hippocampal neurons under basal conditions.
source: The results showed that KIF2C knockdown did not affect spine density (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spine density in control versus KIF2C knockdown neurons showing no significant difference.

claim: Acute knockdown of KIF2C in cultured neurons does not affect basal synaptic transmission.
source: Electrophysiological recordings also showed similar frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory synaptic currents (mEPSCs) in control and knockdown neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C), suggesting that acute knockdown of KIF2C in cultured neurons does not affect basal synaptic transmission.
evidence: Supported by mEPSC recordings showing no significant differences in frequency or amplitude between control and knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C is essential for spine structural plasticity.
source: However, the spine head width significantly increased in control hippocampal neurons, whereas it was not affected in the KIF2C knockdown neurons after cLTP stimulation (Figure 2E), indicating that KIF2C is essential for spine structural plasticity.
evidence: Supported by measurements showing increased spine head width after cLTP in control but not in KIF2C knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C is removed from postsynaptic sites by neuronal activity.
source: In addition, both subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemical results showed that KIF2C was not colocalizing as much with PSD-95 and expressed more in dendritic shafts after cLTP (Figure 2F–I), suggesting a translocation of KIF2C from synaptic protrusions into dendrites.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemistry data showing decreased KIF2C colocalization with PSD-95 after cLTP.

claim: KIF2C knockdown in hippocampal CA1 neurons in vivo results in enhanced mEPSC amplitude.
source: Compared to the control, KIF2C knockdown neurons had enhanced amplitude but similar frequency of mEPSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from acute brain slices showing increased mEPSC amplitude in KIF2C knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C knockdown blocks cLTP-induced increase in mEPSC amplitude.
source: The results showed that mEPSCs amplitude was significantly increased in control hippocampal neurons, whereas it was not affected in the shkif2c neurons after cLTP stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing that cLTP increases mEPSC amplitude in control but not in KIF2C knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C knockdown has minimal effect on presynaptic function.
source: KIF2C knockdown neurons exhibited comparable PPRs to the control, suggesting that KIF2C had a minimal effect on contacting presynaptic function (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements showing no significant difference between control and knockdown neurons.

claim: The NMDAR/AMPAR ratio is decreased in KIF2C knockdown hippocampal slices.
source: In addition, the excitatory postsynaptic current ratio of N-methyl-D-aspartic acid receptor (NMDAR)/α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) was decreased in knockdown hippocampal slices (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements of NMDAR and AMPAR-mediated currents.

claim: AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are increased in KIF2C knockdown neurons.
source: The input-output relationship of NMDAR/AMPAR-mediated EPSCs showed that amplitude of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs under various stimulation intensities was comparable, while AMPAR-mediated EPSCs was increased in KIF2C knockdown neurons (Figure 3D–E), indicating a specific change in AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: Supported by input-output curve measurements showing increased AMPAR-mediated currents at various stimulation intensities.

claim: The magnitude of LTP is significantly attenuated in KIF2C knockdown hippocampal slices.
source: The magnitude of LTP was significantly attenuated in knockdown hippocampal slices (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell LTP recordings showing reduced potentiation in KIF2C knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C is necessary for synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons.
source: These results suggest that KIF2C is necessary for synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons, and its insufficiency may affect the basal function of AMPARs in the hippocampus.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing impaired LTP and altered AMPAR function in KIF2C knockdown neurons.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice display normal body weight and brain size.
source: There were no significant differences in body weight or brain size between kif2cflox/flox;NestinCre (cKO) and kif2cflox/flox (WT) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by measurements of body weight and brain weight showing no significant differences.

claim: The thickness of hippocampal CA1 and CA3 regions does not change significantly in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: In addition, using Nissl staining, we found that the thickness of hippocampal CA1 and CA3 regions did not change significantly in cKO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining and quantification of hippocampal layer thickness.

claim: Dendritic complexity is not significantly different between WT and KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Further examination of neuronal morphology of CA1 pyramidal cells by Golgi staining and Sholl analysis showed no significant differences in dendritic complexity or spine density between WT mice and KIF2C cKO mice (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis showing similar dendritic arborization patterns.

claim: Spine density is not significantly different between WT and KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Further examination of neuronal morphology of CA1 pyramidal cells by Golgi staining and Sholl analysis showed no significant differences in dendritic complexity or spine density between WT mice and KIF2C cKO mice (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spine density from Golgi-stained neurons.

claim: The density of mushroom-type spines decreases in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: However, the density of mushroom-type spines decreased in basal and apical dendrites of hippocampal neurons in cKO mice, whereas the density of filopodia-type spines increased (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by morphological classification and quantification of spine types showing decreased mushroom spine density.

claim: The density of filopodia-type spines increases in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: However, the density of mushroom-type spines decreased in basal and apical dendrites of hippocampal neurons in cKO mice, whereas the density of filopodia-type spines increased (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by morphological classification and quantification showing increased filopodia spine density.

claim: The length and thickness of the PSD fraction are remarkably reduced in the hippocampus of KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Furthermore, electron microscopy analysis revealed that the length and thickness of the PSD fraction were remarkably reduced in the hippocampus of cKO mice (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy measurements of PSD dimensions.

claim: Mushroom spines are commonly considered mature spines.
source: Mushroom spines are commonly considered mature spines (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on spine morphology.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice show impaired spine maturation in the hippocampal CA1 region.
source: Mushroom spines are commonly considered mature spines (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012); therefore, these results indicate impaired spine maturation in the hippocampal CA1 region of cKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the decreased density of mushroom spines and increased filopodia spines in cKO mice.

claim: The amplitude of mEPSCs increases in KIF2C cKO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Consistent with the shRNA knockdown experiments in CA1, the amplitude of mEPSCs increased in cKO mice compared to that in WT controls, whereas the frequency of mEPSCs was similar between the two groups (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs from CA1 pyramidal neurons.

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs is similar between WT and KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Consistent with the shRNA knockdown experiments in CA1, the amplitude of mEPSCs increased in cKO mice compared to that in WT controls, whereas the frequency of mEPSCs was similar between the two groups (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant difference in mEPSC frequency.

claim: The increased mEPSC amplitude in KIF2C cKO mice is not due to altered presynaptic activity.
source: The increased mEPSC amplitude was not due to altered presynaptic activity as the PPRs were not affected in cKO neurons (Figure 5B), indicating a postsynaptic influence in mEPSC property.
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements showing no difference between WT and cKO mice.

claim: The NMDAR/AMPAR ratio is decreased in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Result showed a decreased ratio NMDAR/AMPAR in cKO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements of NMDAR and AMPAR-mediated currents.

claim: AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are increased in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: The amplitude of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was comparable under various stimulation, while AMPAR-mediated EPSCs was increased (Figure 5D–E), indicating a specific defect in AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: Supported by input-output curve measurements showing increased AMPAR currents at various stimulation intensities.

claim: The level of surface AMPA receptors is significantly increased in the KIF2C cKO hippocampus.
source: The level of surface AMPA receptors was significantly increased in the cKO hippocampus (Figure 5F), which coincided with the electrophysiological abnormalities in AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission in cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by cell-surface biotinylation experiments showing increased GluA1 and GluA2 surface expression.

claim: LTP magnitude is significantly attenuated in KIF2C cKO hippocampal slices using single high-frequency stimulation.
source: Result showed that the LTP magnitude was significantly attenuated in cKO hippocampal by two different induction protocols: single high-frequency stimulation (1× HFS) and 4-train LTP (4× HFS) (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by field EPSP recordings showing reduced LTP after 1× HFS in cKO mice.

claim: LTP magnitude is significantly attenuated in KIF2C cKO hippocampal slices using 4-train LTP.
source: Result showed that the LTP magnitude was significantly attenuated in cKO hippocampal by two different induction protocols: single high-frequency stimulation (1× HFS) and 4-train LTP (4× HFS) (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by field EPSP recordings showing reduced LTP after 4× HFS in cKO mice.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) is not altered in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: Long-term depression (LTD) was not altered (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by field EPSP recordings showing similar LTD between WT and cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C plays a critical role in LTP induction and maintenance.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that KIF2C plays a critical role in LTP induction and maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing impaired LTP in KIF2C knockdown and cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C regulates MT dynamics by mediating MT depolymerization in dividing cells.
source: Extensive studies on KIF2C in dividing cells have shown that KIF2C regulates MT dynamics by mediating MT depolymerization (Gorbsky, 2004; Helenius et al., 2006; Knowlton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on KIF2C function in mitotic cells.

claim: Dynamic MTs are involved in regulating dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity.
source: Moreover, dynamic MTs are reported to be involved in regulating dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity (Gu and Zheng, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on MT function in neurons.

claim: The speed of EB3 is increased in KIF2C cKO dendrites.
source: Quantitative results showed that the speed of EB3 was increased in cKO dendrites (WT: 8.9 ± 0.8 μm / min, cKO: 12.4 ± 0.5 μm / min) (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging and quantification of EB3-tdtomato comet dynamics.

claim: Depletion of KIF2C significantly increases MT plus-end growth speed.
source: Depletion of KIF2C significantly increased MT plus-end growth speed (WT: 24.0 ± 1.1 μm / min, cKO: 31.0 ± 1.0 μm / min), and decreased its growth lifetime (WT: 9.4 ± 0.4 s, cKO: 6.7 ± 0.1 s) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by plusTipTracker analysis of EB3-labeled MT plus ends.

claim: Depletion of KIF2C decreases MT plus-end growth lifetime.
source: Depletion of KIF2C significantly increased MT plus-end growth speed (WT: 24.0 ± 1.1 μm / min, cKO: 31.0 ± 1.0 μm / min), and decreased its growth lifetime (WT: 9.4 ± 0.4 s, cKO: 6.7 ± 0.1 s) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by plusTipTracker analysis showing shorter growth lifetime in cKO neurons.

claim: MT plus end growth length is not significantly altered by KIF2C depletion.
source: MT plus end growth length was not significantly altered (WT: 3.1 ± 0.1 μm, cKO: 3.0 ± 0.1 μm) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by plusTipTracker analysis showing no significant difference in growth length.

claim: KIF2C regulates MT depolymerization in hippocampal neurons.
source: These results suggest that KIF2C regulates MT depolymerization in hippocampal neurons and that MT dynamics become disordered with KIF2C deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from measurements of altered MT dynamics in KIF2C cKO neurons.

claim: MT spine invasion frequency is significantly increased in KIF2C cKO neurons.
source: Quantitative results showed that MT spine invasion frequency was increased significantly (Figure 6C) in cKO neurons.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging and kymograph analysis of MT invasion events.

claim: KIF2C deficiency leads to increased MT spine invasion events under basal state.
source: We found that without BDNF treatment, the population of spines containing tyrosinated-α-tubulin was larger in cKO neurons (Figure 6D), suggesting that KIF2C deficiency led to an increased MT spine invasion events under basal state.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry showing more spines containing tyrosinated-α-tubulin in cKO neurons.

claim: MT spine invasion is robustly increased in WT neurons after BDNF treatment.
source: After BDNF treatment, MT spine invasion was robustly increased in WT neurons, while making no change in cKO neurons (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by quantification of spines containing tyrosinated-α-tubulin after BDNF treatment.

claim: KIF2C is required for activity-dependent MT invasion in spines.
source: After BDNF treatment, MT spine invasion was robustly increased in WT neurons, while making no change in cKO neurons (Figure 6D), and such abolished augment could be rescued by re-expression GFP-KIF2C (Figure 6E), indicating that KIF2C is required for the activity-dependent MT invasion in spines.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored BDNF-induced MT invasion with KIF2C re-expression.

claim: KIF2C binds to the end of MTs and couples ATP hydrolysis to initiate MT depolymerization in mitotic cells.
source: In mitotic cells, KIF2C binds to the end of MTs and couples ATP hydrolysis to initiate MT depolymerization (Sanhaji et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on KIF2C mechanism in dividing cells.

claim: The human homologous KIF2C G495A mutant loses ATP hydrolyzing and MT depolymerization abilities.
source: Its human homologous KIF2C G495A mutant has been previously reported to lose ATP hydrolyzing and hence MT depolymerization abilities (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the G495A mutant.

claim: KIF2C(G491A) transfected cells have intact cell morphology.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis showed that KIF2C(G491A) transfected cells had intact cell morphology, while the KIF2C(WT) successfully depolymerized MTs and maintained cell rounding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry of HEK 293T cells transfected with KIF2C constructs.

claim: KIF2C(WT) successfully depolymerizes MTs and maintains cell rounding in transfected cells.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis showed that KIF2C(G491A) transfected cells had intact cell morphology, while the KIF2C(WT) successfully depolymerized MTs and maintained cell rounding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry showing disrupted MT network in KIF2C(WT) transfected cells.

claim: Re-expression of KIF2C(WT) significantly reduces the elevated amplitude of mEPSCs in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: The results showed that re-expression of KIF2C(WT) significantly reduced the elevated amplitude of mEPSCs (Figure 6F) and restored LTP in cKO mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from cKO mice with KIF2C(WT) re-expression.

claim: Re-expression of KIF2C(WT) restores LTP in KIF2C cKO mice.
source: The results showed that re-expression of KIF2C(WT) significantly reduced the elevated amplitude of mEPSCs (Figure 6F) and restored LTP in cKO mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by field EPSP recordings showing restored LTP with KIF2C(WT) re-expression.

claim: The KIF2C(G491A) mutant fails to show significant differences in mEPSC properties in cKO CA1 neurons.
source: However, without MT depolymerization activity, the KIF2C (G491A) mutant failed to show significant differences in mEPSC properties (Figure 6F) or LTP induction in the cKO CA1 neurons (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no rescue effect with KIF2C(G491A).

claim: The KIF2C(G491A) mutant fails to rescue LTP induction in cKO CA1 neurons.
source: However, without MT depolymerization activity, the KIF2C (G491A) mutant failed to show significant differences in mEPSC properties (Figure 6F) or LTP induction in the cKO CA1 neurons (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by field EPSP recordings showing no LTP rescue with KIF2C(G491A).

claim: KIF2C regulates synaptic transmission and plasticity by mediating dynamic MT depolymerization in dendrites and spines.
source: These findings indicate that KIF2C regulates synaptic transmission and plasticity by mediating dynamic MT depolymerization in dendrites and spines.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing that only functional KIF2C(WT) but not the depolymerization-defective mutant can restore synaptic function.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice show normal motion and anxiety levels in the open field test and elevated zero maze.
source: The KIF2C cKO mice showed normal motion and anxiety levels in the open field test and elevated zero maze compared to those of the WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements showing no significant differences in locomotion and anxiety-related behaviors.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice have normal grooming frequencies in the repetitive behavioral test.
source: The KIF2C cKO mice showed normal motion and anxiety levels in the open field test and elevated zero maze compared to those of the WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), and had normal grooming frequencies in the commonly used repetitive behavioral test (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by self-grooming test showing no significant difference between WT and cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C cKO and WT mice show similar learning curves and probe performance in the Morris water maze task.
source: The Morris water maze task also elicited similar learning curves and probe performance in both KIF2C cKO and WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), suggesting normal spatial learning and memory ability in mice with KIF2C deficiency.
evidence: Supported by Morris water maze test showing no significant differences in spatial learning and memory.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice show significant impairment in spontaneous alternation behavior in the Y-maze test.
source: However, when we subjected the mice to the Y-maze test, KIF2C cKO mice showed significant impairment in spontaneous alternation behavior compared to that of the WT mice (Figure 7A), indicating that KIF2C cKO mice were deficient in short working memory
evidence: Supported by Y-maze test showing decreased spontaneous alternation in cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice are deficient in short working memory.
source: However, when we subjected the mice to the Y-maze test, KIF2C cKO mice showed significant impairment in spontaneous alternation behavior compared to that of the WT mice (Figure 7A), indicating that KIF2C cKO mice were deficient in short working memory
evidence: Inferred from impaired spontaneous alternation behavior in Y-maze test.

claim: CA1 has a special role in temporal processing.
source: indicating that KIF2C cKO mice were deficient in short working memory, which could be due to the special role of CA1 in temporal processing (Hoge and Kesner, 2007; Ji and Maren, 2008; Farovik et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on CA1 function.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice display a comparatively weaker freezing response to context and tone conditioned stimulus during fear conditioning acquisition.
source: The conditioned fear learning test showed that KIF2C cKO mice displayed a comparatively weaker freezing response to the context and tone conditioned stimulus (CS) during the acquisition stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by cued fear conditioning test showing reduced freezing during acquisition.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice show less freezing time compared to WT mice in context-dependent and CS-dependent fear memory tests.
source: We monitored the conditioned freezing response to the background context and CS until seven or 8 days after acquisition, respectively, and found that cKO mice still showed less freezing time compared to WT mice, particularly in context-dependent freezing (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by fear conditioning test showing reduced freezing in cKO mice at multiple time points.

claim: Fear memory in KIF2C cKO mice is impaired.
source: These results suggest that fear memory in KIF2C cKO mice was impaired.
evidence: Inferred from reduced freezing responses in fear conditioning tests.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice have intact fear memory maintenance.
source: The percentage change in freezing time between the KIF2C WT and cKO mice showed no significant difference, indicating an intact fear memory maintenance in cKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of percentage change in freezing time showing no significant difference.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice have normal sensorimotor gating.
source: In a prepulse inhibition test, WT and cKO mice showed the same extent of inhibition as the prepulse (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), showing that the cKO mice had normal sensorimotor gating.
evidence: Supported by prepulse inhibition test showing no significant difference between WT and cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice exhibit normal sociability.
source: KIF2C cKO mice exhibited a normal preference for the chamber in which a stranger mouse (S1) was present, compared with the empty chamber (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by three-chamber social test showing normal preference for stranger mouse over empty chamber.

claim: KIF2C cKO mice exhibit significantly reduced social novelty.
source: However, with the introduction of a second stranger (S2), KIF2C cKO mice exhibited no preference for the novel stranger (S2), compared with the familiar mouse (S1) (Figure 7E). These results showed that KIF2C cKO mice showed normal sociability but significantly reduced social novelty
evidence: Supported by three-chamber social test showing no preference for novel stranger in cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C is essential for social memory maintenance.
source: These results showed that KIF2C cKO mice showed normal sociability but significantly reduced social novelty, indicating that KIF2C is essential for social memory maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from impaired social novelty preference in cKO mice.

claim: KIF2C plays an important role in CA1-mediated cognitive and memory functions.
source: Based on the behavioral tests, we found that KIF2C plays an important role in CA1-mediated cognitive and memory functions.
evidence: Inferred from multiple behavioral deficits observed in KIF2C cKO mice.

claim: The deficiencies observed in behavioral tests of KIF2C cKO mice are highly likely due to the lack of LTP in the CA1 region.
source: The deficiencies observed in the Y-maze test, cued conditioned fear memory, and three-chambered social test of KIF2C cKO mice were highly likely due to the lack of LTP in the CA1 region (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Inferred from correlation between impaired LTP and behavioral deficits.

claim: Over-expression of KIF2C in mice for a long time leads to neuronal death.
source: In our pretests, over-expression of KIF2C in mice for a long time would lead to neuronal death (data not shown).
evidence: Mentioned as unpublished observation from pretests.

claim: cKO mice with KIF2C(WT) re-expression display normal alternation in the Y-maze test.
source: The results showed that cKO mice with KIF2C(WT) re-expression displayed a normal alternation in the Y-maze test compared to cKO mice with control virus (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by Y-maze test showing rescued spontaneous alternation with KIF2C(WT) re-expression.

claim: cKO mice with KIF2C(WT) re-expression show normal interaction with the stranger mouse in the social novelty test.
source: Furthermore, cKO mice with KIF2C(WT) re-expression also showed normal interaction with the stranger mouse in the social novelty test (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: Supported by three-chamber social test showing rescued social novelty preference with KIF2C(WT) re-expression.

claim: cKO mice injected with KIF2C(G491A) virus show impaired working and social memory.
source: The results showed that cKO mice injected with KIF2C(G491A) virus still showed impaired working and social memory (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by Y-maze and three-chamber social tests showing no rescue with KIF2C(G491A).

claim: KIF2C is critical for cognitive function, mediated by its MT depolymerization ability in synapses during LTP.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that KIF2C is critical for cognitive function, and this functional role is mediated by its MT depolymerization ability in synapses during LTP.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing that only functional KIF2C(WT) but not the mutant can restore cognitive behaviors.

claim: KIF2C is an ATP-dependent MT depolymerization factor that functions in several mitotic processes.
source: KIF2C is an ATP-dependent MT depolymerization factor that functions in several mitotic processes, such as spindle assembly, MT dynamics, correct kinetochore-MT attachment, and chromosome positioning and segregation (Sanhaji et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on KIF2C function in mitosis.

claim: The function of KIF2C in the CNS was largely unknown prior to this study.
source: However, its function in the CNS was largely unknown.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge before this study.

claim: This study elucidated the functions of KIF2C in regulating spine morphology, synaptic transmission, and plasticity in hippocampal neurons.
source: Our study elucidated the functions of KIF2C in regulating spine morphology, synaptic transmission, and plasticity in hippocampal neurons and its critical role in CA1-mediated cognitive behaviors.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: This study unveils the critical role of KIF2C in the CNS, showing that its known function in regulating dynamic MT stability also takes place in neurons.
source: Our study unveils the critical role of KIF2C in the CNS, showing that its known function in regulating dynamic MT stability also takes place in neurons.
evidence: Summary statement connecting KIF2C's known mitotic function to its neuronal function.

claim: KIF2C deficiency has higher impact on synaptic structure plasticity than on spine formation.
source: According to our results, KIF2C deficiency seems to have higher impact on synaptic structure plasticity than that on spine formation, which provides a link between dynamic MT stability and synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Inferred from observations that spine density is normal but spine morphology and plasticity are impaired in KIF2C deficient neurons.

claim: Both acute knockdown and genetic deficiency of KIF2C eliminate LTP but not LTD expression.
source: We have also found that both acute knockdown or genetic deficiency of KIF2C eliminated LTP but not LTD expression.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Increased expression of ionic glutamate receptors, particularly AMPARs, on synapses may lead to LTP occlusion in KIF2C deficient neurons.
source: It is possible that increased expression of ionic glutamate receptors, particularly AMPARs, on synapses leads to LTP occlusion.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed LTP impairment based on increased AMPAR surface expression.

claim: KIF2C might be involved in the expression and/or transportation of synaptic substances for LTP long-lasting maintenance.
source: Moreover, 4-train LTP impairment in cKO mice, which requires further gene transcription and protein synthesis in the postsynaptic neuron, suggests that KIF2C might also be involved in the expression and/or transportation of synaptic substances for LTP long-lasting maintenance.
evidence: Speculative inference from 4-train LTP impairment which requires protein synthesis.

claim: NMDA receptors can be transported by KIF17 along MTs in dendrites.
source: It has been reported that NMDA receptors can be transported by KIF17 (Setou et al., 2000) and AMPA receptors can be transported by KIF5 along MTs in dendrites (Setou et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on receptor trafficking.

claim: AMPA receptors can be transported by KIF5 along MTs in dendrites.
source: It has been reported that NMDA receptors can be transported by KIF17 (Setou et al., 2000) and AMPA receptors can be transported by KIF5 along MTs in dendrites (Setou et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on receptor trafficking.

claim: KIF2C may regulate membrane receptor trafficking by mediating MT dynamics through the regulation of MT stability.
source: It is possible that KIF2C regulates membrane receptor trafficking by mediating MT dynamics through the regulation of MT stability.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed based on known functions of MTs in receptor trafficking.

claim: MT dynamic stability regulates AMPARs postsynaptic localization and synaptic plasticity.
source: Furthermore, MT dynamic stability regulates AMPARs postsynaptic localization and synaptic plasticity (McVicker et al., 2016; Uchida et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on MT regulation of AMPAR localization.

claim: MT-dependent trafficking of AMPARs has been typically associated with long-range transport along dendrites.
source: In the case of AMPARs trafficking, MT-dependent trafficking has been typically associated with long-range transport along the dendrites, supporting the continuous supply and redistribution of AMPARs among synapses (Hoerndli et al., 2013; Heisler et al., 2014), which can also be regulated by neuronal activity (Hoerndli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on AMPAR trafficking mechanisms.

claim: KIF2C may confine AMPARs' trafficking to the synaptic site through MT depolymerization and stability.
source: We speculate that KIF2C may also confine the AMPARs' trafficking to the synaptic site through MT depolymerization and stability.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed based on KIF2C's MT depolymerization function and AMPAR trafficking.

claim: Translocation of KIF2C out from synapse during synaptic activation may be required to ensure robust MT invasion into spines.
source: It is possible that translocation of KIF2C out from synapse or depletion of synaptic KIF2C during synaptic activation is required to ensure robust MT invasion into spines, where and MT depolymerization should be inhibited.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed based on observed KIF2C translocation after cLTP.

claim: Oligomeric amyloid-β directly inhibits the MT-dependent ATPase activity of KIF2C in vitro.
source: Interestingly, Oligomeric amyloid-β directly inhibits the MT-dependent ATPase activity of KIF2C in vitro, and thereby leads to the generation of defective mitotic structures which may contributes to the development of Alzheimer's disease (Borysov et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Aβ effects on KIF2C.

claim: Aβ stabilizes MT by reducing catastrophe-frequency.
source: Aβ stabilizes MT by reducing catastrophe-frequency (Qu et al., 2017), which is similar with KIF2C conditional knockout phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature and comparison to observed KIF2C cKO phenotype.

claim: KIF2C was recently discovered as a blood biomarker for suicidal ideation in psychiatric patients.
source: Furthermore, KIF2C was recently discovered as a blood biomarker for suicidal ideation in psychiatric patients, such as patients with schizophrenia (Niculescu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical study on KIF2C as biomarker.

claim: KIF2C could be a therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease or suicidality psychiatric disorders.
source: Therefore, KIF2C could be a therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease or suicidality psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on associations between KIF2C and these disorders.

claim: Microtubules are eukaryotic cytoskeletons that play an important role in cell function.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are eukaryotic cytoskeletons that play an important role in cell function.
evidence: General statement of established knowledge about microtubules.

claim: In the central nervous system, MTs serve as a structural basis for trafficking material throughout the neuron.
source: In the central nervous system, MTs serve as a structural basis for trafficking material throughout the neuron and are the primary regulators of neuronal differentiation (Dent and Baas, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on MT function in neurons.

claim: MTs are the primary regulators of neuronal differentiation.
source: In the central nervous system, MTs serve as a structural basis for trafficking material throughout the neuron and are the primary regulators of neuronal differentiation (Dent and Baas, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on MT function in neuronal development.

claim: MT dynamic instability has been detected in both shaft and dendritic protrusions.
source: The MTs dynamic instability, that is the growing or shrinking of MT plus end, has been detected in both shaft and dendritic protrusions (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984) and is involved in spine formation and synaptic function (Hu et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2008; Merriam et al., 2011; Tada and Sheng, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on MT dynamics in neurons.

claim: MT dynamic instability is involved in spine formation and synaptic function.
source: The MTs dynamic instability, that is the growing or shrinking of MT plus end, has been detected in both shaft and dendritic protrusions (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984) and is involved in spine formation and synaptic function (Hu et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2008; Merriam et al., 2011; Tada and Sheng, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on MT function in synapses.

claim: Inhibition of MT polymerization results in deficits in long-term potentiation.
source: Inhibition of MT polymerization results in deficits in long-term potentiation (LTP) and negatively affects memory formation or retention (Shumyatsky et al., 2005; Jaworski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on MT polymerization and LTP.

claim: Inhibition of MT polymerization negatively affects memory formation or retention.
source: Inhibition of MT polymerization results in deficits in long-term potentiation (LTP) and negatively affects memory formation or retention (Shumyatsky et al., 2005; Jaworski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on MT polymerization and memory.

claim: Abnormal MT dynamics is associated with several neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases.
source: The abnormal MTs dynamics is associated with several neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, and depression (Brunden et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on MT dysfunction in disease.

claim: During neuronal activities, MTs can be regulated to extend from the dendritic shaft into spines and affect synaptic structure and function.
source: During neuronal activities, MTs can be regulated to extend from the dendritic shaft into spines and affect synaptic structure and function (3-8), which could be an important event for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Statement about MT invasion into spines during neuronal activity, with implied citations.

claim: The regulatory mechanism underlying MT dynamics in or out from synapse upon neuronal activity is still unclear.
source: However, regulatory mechanism underlying MT dynamics in or out from synapse upon neuronal activity is still unclear, nor its role in learning and memory.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: The kinesin-13 family has a distinct function in depolymerizing MTs.
source: The kinesin-13 family of kinesin superfamily proteins (KIFs) has a distinct function in depolymerizing MTs (Howard and Hyman, 2007), and therefore is involved in many MT-dependent events (Kline-Smith et al., 2004; Homma et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on kinesin-13 family function.

claim: KIF2C is the best-characterized member of the kinesin-13 family.
source: KIF2C, also called mitotic centromere-associated kinesin (MCAK), is the best-characterized family member and is localized to the spindle poles, spindle midzone, and kinetochores in dividing cells.
evidence: Statement about KIF2C's characterization status in the literature.

claim: KIF2C is localized to the spindle poles, spindle midzone, and kinetochores in dividing cells.
source: KIF2C, also called mitotic centromere-associated kinesin (MCAK), is the best-characterized family member and is localized to the spindle poles, spindle midzone, and kinetochores in dividing cells.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about KIF2C localization in mitotic cells.

claim: KIF2C utilizes MT depolymerase activity to regulate spindle formation and correct inappropriate MT attachments at kinetochores.
source: KIF2C utilizes MT depolymerase activity to regulate spindle formation and correct inappropriate MT attachments at kinetochores (Gorbsky, 2004; Helenius et al., 2006; Knowlton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on KIF2C function in mitosis.

claim: KIF2C uses ATP hydrolysis for MT depolymerization from both ends.
source: KIF2C uses ATP hydrolysis for MT depolymerization from both ends and directly interacts with EBs to enhance its destabilizing ability (Wordeman, 2005; Walczak, 2003; Wang et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on KIF2C mechanism.

claim: KIF2C directly interacts with EBs to enhance its destabilizing ability.
source: KIF2C uses ATP hydrolysis for MT depolymerization from both ends and directly interacts with EBs to enhance its destabilizing ability (Wordeman, 2005; Walczak, 2003; Wang et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on KIF2C-EB interaction.

claim: KIF2C is associated with Alzheimer's disease and suicidality psychiatric disorders.
source: Particularly, KIF2C is associated with Alzheimer's disease and suicidality psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Statement about clinical associations, supported by subsequent citations in the text.

claim: KIF2C is significantly decreased in suicidal ideation cohort.
source: Clinical evidence shows that KIF2C is significantly decreased in suicidal ideation cohort and could be utilized as a reference for predicting suicidality (Niculescu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical study.

claim: The in vivo physiological function of KIF2C in the CNS remained to be elucidated prior to this study.
source: However, the in vivo physiological function of KIF2C in the CNS remains to be elucidated.
evidence: Statement about the knowledge gap that this study addresses.
